Note.Name: README
Note.Text:
## Overview

This repository contains the Forsta integration for Research Defender (RD). It
wraps both the client-side scripts that call the RD APIs and the server-side
logic that verifies responses and determines whether a respondent can continue
through the survey.

At a high level the integration:

- Collects RD Search V4 and RD Activity data into two Forsta text-list
  questions, `RD_Search` and `RD_Activity`.
- Validates and hashes RD Search data on the server before trusting the client
  payload.
- Retrieves RD Activity statistics server-side using an API token obtained in
  the browser.
- Aggregates the outcomes into a single-value question
  `research_defender_fail` where `0 = allow respondent to continue`,
  `1 = terminate respondent`.

## Configuration

The implementation is configured in the `consts` script. There are two steps
for configuration the project:

1. Fill in the `projectSettings` object (see comments for instructions)
2. Uncomment one of the template configs depending on the type of project.
   It is vital that this is set selected correctly because all of the termination
   logic depens on the values of this config. The defaults align with the company
   standard settings: 
   https://srcentre.sharepoint.com/:w:/s/AuditRiskandPrivacyCommittee/IQCcJahzDWdjRKFloXNC2qfeASJqFJQ_sPub2XwMWw4XtuQ?e=sUGs8X


## Data flow

1. Landing page (`client/onlineIntro.js`) unhides the intro content and the 
   next button only when RD calls finish. It listens for custom events fired by
   the producer scripts so the respondent cannot continue until responses are
   available.
2. **RD Search (`client/search.js`)** runs client-side, calls the RD Search V4
   endpoint, stores the raw payload and HTTP status into `RD_Search`, then fires
   the completion event.
3. **RD Activity token fetch (`client/activity.js`)** runs client-side, calls the
   RD Activity token endpoint, stores the raw token payload and HTTP status into
   `RD_Activity`, then fires its completion event.
4. **Server script (`rd.js`)** executes after the page submits. It parses and
   validates `RD_Search` via `processSearchResults()`, pulls statistics for
   `RD_Activity` via `processActivityResults()`, and finally computes
   `research_defender_fail` inside `determineOverallPassFail()`.

## Client-side behaviour

### search.js

- Uses `fetch` with credentials and an 8-second timeout supplied by Forsta macros
  (`^getTimeout()^`, `^makeRDSearchURL()^`).
- Writes `status_code` and `raw_response` to `RD_Search`.
- Emits a custom event (`^getSearchEventName()^`) so the intro screen can
  re-enable navigation.

### activity.js

- Calls the RD Activity token endpoint with the public API key. Response text
  goes into `RD_Activity.raw_token_response`, HTTP status into `status_code`.
- Emits a second custom event (`^getActivityEventName()^`) and unhides the intro
  once both events are received.

### onlineIntro.js

- Waits for both events (or detects prefilled hidden inputs) before restoring
  the original intro content and un-hiding buttons, preventing users from
  skipping the RD checks.

## Security considerations

The RD Search V4 endpoint supports signing the request URL with the private key
so Research Defender can confirm it was not tampered with. RD also signs the
response payload: `Validation.Surveys` and `Validation.Respondent` are hashes of
the corresponding entries in the `String` object. Because those string values are
not valid JSON, we extract key-value pairs via regular expressions to ensure the
data we trust matches what was signed. We should pursue a native, structured
response with RD to avoid depending on this workaround.

## HTTP status codes and timeouts

Both client scripts use an 8-second timeout. If a request does not complete in
time, it is aborted; the server interprets this as a failure since allowing the
respondent through would let malicious users block outbound traffic to bypass
screening. Every response captures the HTTP status code so we can differentiate
between network issues and valid RD denials.

Hello and welcome back!

Thanks so much for taking part in our study exploring internet use among young people and the social media law. This survey is the next step in the study. You may remember completing the first survey at the end of last year, and some families were also invited to complete a short follow-up earlier this year. Whether or not you took part in that, your participation now is just as important and valuable.

We’re very grateful for you taking the time to share your thoughts and experiences with us!

Before you get started, the Participant Information Sheet below has some information about the project.

To see this Information Sheet, click here

This survey will take you about 20 minutes to complete. We will then ask your child to complete their part of the survey, which will also take about 20 minutes.

Your answers will be kept private – meaning we won’t name you in our survey reports or anywhere else and we won’t include any information that might mean people could guess who you are.

If at any time during the survey you don’t want to answer a question, you can skip it, and you will have the option to respond with ‘not sure’ or ‘prefer not to say’.

This study has been reviewed and approved by the Australian Institute for Family Studies (AIFS) Human Research Ethics Committee (approval number: 2025/06).

The Ethics Approval process requires you to be provided with a Participant Information Sheet and Consent Form. In order to continue with the survey, you need to first access this statement by clicking the link above.

  • I have read the Participant Information Statement provided.
  • I understand the purpose, activities, time required, and possible risks of participating in this research.
  • I have had the opportunity to ask questions and am satisfied with the answers I received.
  • I understand that the survey isn’t being monitored in real time, so the answers my child and I provide may not be read by the researchers for a few months.
  • I understand that I don’t have to answer any questions I don’t want to.
  • I freely agree to my child’s participation in this research as described in the Participant Information Sheet and understand that my child is free to withdraw at any time during the research.
  • I agree to be the point of contact if my child agrees to be contacted regarding participation in the follow-up surveys.
  • I understand that I can download or print a copy of this document to keep.
Please click ‘I agree’ below to confirm that you would like to do the survey:

FormText.Text:
Thank you for agreeing to take part!

There are no right or wrong answers in this survey, our goal is to learn about you and your family. We are looking forward to hearing what you have to say, and ask that you be as honest as possible when you answer our questions.

Remember, all data collected for this project will remain confidential, except as required by law or if we have serious concerns about someone’s immediate safety.

Also, please remember that there are no penalties for children who are still using social media, nor their parents. We know different families have different views on the age restrictions and we’re not here to judge or to report anyone. Your honest answers will help us understand how social media age restrictions affect families like yours.

Some questions in this survey are very similar to those from the first survey. This is intentional – asking the same questions over time helps us see how things may be changing for you and your child as the law rolls out.

Important - we can only use the answers you give if your child, ^f('SELECTED_CHILD_NICKNAME')^, also completes their part of the survey. This should be the same child who completed the original survey last year. Please make sure they are happy to do this before you go ahead. When you finish answering the questions we have for you, we will ask you to hand over to your child who will complete their own survey.

FormText.Text:
In a previous survey some families were able to provide consent for data linkage at the time, by completing the relevant forms, while others who were interested weren’t able to fully complete the consent process.

We know there are a number of reasons why this could happen – some participants have told us they missed the emails, others might have changed their mind, and others might have started filling out the form but weren't able to finish.

In case this applies to you, we wanted to give you another opportunity to review the information and decide whether you would like to provide consent now.

Taking part in data linkage is completely optional - the decision is entirely up to you and your child. If you’re no longer interested, that’s absolutely fine. If you do decide to take part, we will pay you $5 in recognition of your/your child’s time completing the form.

If you have already signed up and received your $5 incentive, thank you — we really appreciate your involvement. You can check the “My child is already signed up” box on the forms and move on.

If you didn’t receive the $5 incentive, it may mean the form wasn’t fully completed or submitted last time. You can complete it now if you choose to.

Can’t remember?

It was a while ago that we first asked you about this, and there were a lot of parts of the study to get your ahead around! We know that it may be difficult to remember whether you previously completed the consent form. To protect your privacy, consent records are stored separately from survey responses, so we’re not able to display your previous choice within this survey.

If you are unsure whether you completed the form, we recommend you review the consent form, which will be displayed on the coming pages.

In a previous survey some families provided consent for data linkage at that time, while others, like you, said they weren’t interested.

Taking part in data linkage is completely optional - the decision is entirely up to you and your child.

In case you have changed your mind, we wanted to give you another opportunity to review the information and decide whether you would like to provide consent now.

If you previously said no, and haven’t changed your mind, we respect your choice. Just skip through the information on the next couple of pages and check the “I do not agree” box again and proceed to complete the survey.

If you’d like to reconsider, the next few pages will provide a bit more information about data linkage that can help to inform your decision.

What is data linkage and why does it matter?

In this study, data linkage means securely connecting information about your child from different sources, such as school and health records, to their survey responses.

Data linkage strengthens this study by helping us understand whether the law is making a meaningful difference to young people’s wellbeing over time across health, education, and broader life outcomes. By choosing to provide consent (if this feels right for you and your family), you can help contribute to the first evidence base of its kind to inform how the social media law affects young people now and into the future.

All linked data are used only for research, protected by strict privacy laws, and reported in ways that never identify individual children or families.

On the next few pages, you will see separate consent forms for education and health data. These forms are kept separate because they relate to different types of records and consent requirements. They may seem a little repetitive, but we really appreciate you taking the time to carefully consider each one and complete them, if you choose to do so.

We are providing information about data linkage so that both you and your child can make an informed decision. We are seeking:

Your informed consent, which means that you understand what we’re asking and agree that it’s okay for us to link your child’s records.

Your child’s informed assent, which means they understand what we’re asking and agree to it because they feel comfortable with it.

If either of you says no, we will not link your child’s records. And if you or your child changes your mind later, that’s completely fine—just let us know.
